chunks: Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Asim ibn Humayd and al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Asim ibn Humayd, from Abi Basir, from Abi Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about the zakat (alms-tax) of camels, and he said: 'There is no zakat in fewer than five camels. When there are five, there is one sheep, up to ten. When there are ten, there are two sheep, up to fifteen. When there are fifteen, there are three sheep, up to twenty. When there are twenty, there are four sheep, up to twenty-five. When there are twenty-five, there are five sheep. If one more is added, there is an ibn makhad (a young female camel that has entered its fourth year) up to thirty-five. If there is no ibn makhad, then a ibn labun (a young male camel that has entered its fifth year). If one more is added to thirty-five, there is an ibn labun (female) up to forty-five. If one more is added, there is a hiqqah (a three-year-old female camel) up to sixty. If one more is added, there is a jadh'ah (a four-year-old female camel) up to seventy-five. If one more is added, there are two ibn labun (females) up to ninety. If one more is added, there are two hiqqah up to one hundred and twenty. When the camels become numerous, for every fifty camels, one hiqqah is due. And a old (herim) camel is not taken, nor one with a defect (dhawt 'awar), unless the collector wishes to count the young and the old together.'

key_terms.ابْنَةُ مَخَاضٍ: A young female camel that has entered its fourth year
key_terms.ابْنُ لَبُونٍ: A young camel that has entered its fifth year

ai.seo_question: What is the zakat ruling for camels in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* provides the detailed jurisprudential framework for camel zakat, establishing the nisab and specific liability tiers that form the basis of Shia fiqh in this domain. It emphasizes the principle of selecting healthy, prime animals while excluding the weak or defective (*mu'awwar*), reflecting the practical application of divine command in economic purification. The narration underscores the precision required in calculating religious dues, linking material wealth to spiritual accountability through structured, graduated obligations.
